title: Production ML Pipeline
interviewAnswer: A production ML pipeline reliably connects data ingestion and validation to preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, deployment, inference and monitoring. The key difference from a notebook is repeatability, observability and failure handling.
why: This is the bridge from “I can train a model” to “I can operate a reliable ML product.”
intuition: Think of two connected loops: the training loop produces a versioned model artifact; the serving loop loads that artifact to produce predictions. Monitoring feeds evidence back into the next training iteration.
deepDive: A mature pipeline covers ingestion/validation, preprocessing, training, evaluation gates, experiment tracking, model registry, packaging, deployment, inference, observability and rollback. Some systems add feature stores, labeling queues and automated retraining; only add complexity when requirements justify it.
math: No single equation—the key is interface contracts and reproducibility across stages.
code:
# Conceptual stages
validate_data()
X = preprocess(raw)
model = train(X)
metrics = evaluate(model, validation)
if passes_gate(metrics):
    version = registry.register(model, metrics)
    deploy(version)
monitor(version)
commonMistakes: Drawing a pipeline that ends at “deploy model” with no monitoring/rollback.
Putting training notebooks directly behind an API.
Recomputing preprocessing differently at serving time.
production: Keep training and serving contracts explicit. Version artifacts, define SLOs, centralize logs/metrics, and design rollback before the first risky release.
workedExample: For a heavy 3D reconstruction model, the production serving path may be an asynchronous GPU batch job rather than a low-latency endpoint.

lab.goal: Sketch a reproducible train/register/serve contract with explicit artifacts.

visual.title: Production ML lifecycle
visual.caption: Production ML is a continuous system around the model, not only a training script.
